# Baghdad 830 – Mathematics & measurement

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from eras/islamic-830-baghdad.yaml — do not edit -->

K = knowledge level · use = none/wrong/partial/correct · make = producibility with local means · accept = acceptance.

- **Zero and positional notation** [`zero_place_value`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/zero_place_value.md) — K2, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Indian decimal place value with a written zero (sifr, 'empty') has just been set out in Arabic by al-Khwarizmi, c. 825. Astronomers use sexagesimal places in tables. The secretaries of the diwans still reckon on their fingers and write sums out in words. Local: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi; astronomers of the Shammasiyya observations. Elsewhere: India (place value with zero since the 5th–7th c.).
- **Hindu-Arabic numerals and written arithmetic** [`arabic_numerals`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/arabic_numerals.md) — K2, use partial, make easy, accept low. The Indian figures are worked on a dust board (takht) with sand and erased as you go, which makes them suspect to clerks who need a record that cannot be altered. Pen-and-paper Indian arithmetic is a century away (al-Uqlidisi, c. 952). Paper is already cheap here, so the method can be skipped ahead. Local: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (book on Indian reckoning); katibs of the diwan of the kharaj.
- **Abacus and counting board** [`abacus_counting_board`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/abacus_counting_board.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Clerks reckon by finger positions (hisab al-yad, 'arithmetic of the hand') and in their heads; letters of the abjad stand for numbers in astronomy. The Indian dust board is the scholars' tool. No bead frame. Local: katibs of the diwans. Elsewhere: China (counting rods); Byzantium (pebble boards).
- **Common fractions and the rule of three** [`fractions_rule_of_three`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/fractions_rule_of_three.md) — K3, use correct, make easy, accept high. Clerks express fractions in the Arabic named fractions (a half, a third ... a tenth) and their products, astronomers in sexagesimal minutes and seconds. The rule of three is in the Sindhind and used daily for inheritance shares, which Islamic law makes an arithmetic problem. Local: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (inheritance problems in al-Jabr); qadis and faradi (inheritance reckoners).
- **Decimal fractions** [`decimal_fractions`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/decimal_fractions.md) — K0, use none, make easy, accept medium. Not yet in use; fractions are named, unit-based or sexagesimal. With decimal place value just arriving, the extension to tenths is one sentence for a player and easy to show on the dust board.
- **Negative numbers** [`negative_numbers`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/negative_numbers.md) — K1, use none, make easy, accept low. Brahmagupta's rules for 'fortunes and debts' sit inside the Indian astronomy behind the Sindhind, but nobody here takes them up. Al-Khwarizmi subtracts terms ('what is lacking') without accepting a negative answer. Local: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi. Elsewhere: India (Brahmagupta, 628); China (red and black rods).
- **Square roots and irrational numbers** [`square_roots_irrationals`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/square_roots_irrationals.md) — K3, use correct, make easy, accept medium. Root extraction is taught in Indian reckoning and needed in al-Jabr. Euclid book 10 on irrational magnitudes is in al-Hajjaj's translation, read by very few. Roots are approximated and treated as magnitudes, not numbers. Local: al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf ibn Matar (Euclid); Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi.
- **Logarithms** [`logarithms`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/logarithms.md) — K0, use none, make medium, accept medium. Astronomers multiply large sexagesimal numbers by hand for every table; a table that turns products into sums would be welcomed at once by the observatory staff. Local: Habash al-Hasib and the astronomers of the Mumtahan tables.
- **Slide rule** [`slide_rule`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/slide_rule.md) — K0, use none, make medium, accept low
- **Symbolic algebra** [`symbolic_algebra`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/symbolic_algebra.md) — K2, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Al-Jabr is brand new, written entirely in words ('a square and ten roots equal thirty-nine dirhams'). Its names, shay' (thing), jidhr (root), mal (wealth, the square), are the beginning of a vocabulary. Short symbols would be new; an Indian abbreviation by syllables exists in Brahmagupta. Local: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (al-Kitab al-mukhtasar fi hisab al-jabr wa'l-muqabala, c. 820s). Elsewhere: India (Brahmagupta's colour-syllable abbreviations).
- **Solving quadratic and cubic equations** [`quadratic_cubic_equations`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/quadratic_cubic_equations.md) — K3, use correct, make easy, accept high. Al-Khwarizmi's six standard forms with rules and geometric proofs by completing the square are the newest mathematics in the world, dedicated to al-Ma'mun. Only positive roots count. Cubics are unsolved (Omar Khayyam will solve them geometrically c. 1070). Local: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi.
- **Systems of linear equations (elimination and matrices)** [`linear_equations_matrices`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/linear_equations_matrices.md) — K1, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Problems with several unknowns are solved one by one with words and the rule of false position. Systematic elimination on a grid is a Chinese method nobody here has seen. Elsewhere: China (Nine Chapters, fangcheng).
- **Complex numbers** [`complex_numbers`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/complex_numbers.md) — K0, use none, make easy, accept low. A negative under a root means the problem 'is impossible'; al-Khwarizmi says so of the equation with no solution.
- **Prime numbers and number theory** [`prime_numbers_number_theory`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/prime_numbers_number_theory.md) — K2, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Euclid's arithmetic books (7–9) with the infinity of primes are in Arabic. Nicomachus' Introduction to Arithmetic is known through Syriac; Thabit ibn Qurra, who will translate it and find the rule for amicable numbers, is a small child in Harran. Local: al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf ibn Matar. Elsewhere: Harran (Thabit ibn Qurra, born 826 or 836).
- **Combinatorics (permutations, combinations, Pascal's triangle)** [`combinatorics_permutations`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/combinatorics_permutations.md) — K2, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad (d. c. 786–791) built his dictionary Kitab al-Ayn by permuting every root of two to five letters, a counting of arrangements every philologist knows. Binomial coefficients are not yet tabulated. Local: grammarians of Basra and Kufa; al-Khalil's Kitab al-Ayn. Elsewhere: India (Pingala's metres).
- **Compound interest and exponential growth** [`compound_interest_exponential_growth`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/compound_interest_exponential_growth.md) — K1, use none, make easy, accept low. Interest (riba) is forbidden in law, so nobody compounds it openly. Chess (shatranj) is the fashion at court, and the doubling-grains story belongs to it, but in surviving Arabic texts only later.
- **Deductive geometry and proof (Euclid, Pythagoras)** [`geometry_proof`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/geometry_proof.md) — K3, use correct, make easy, accept high. Euclid has been translated twice by al-Hajjaj ibn Matar (for Harun and again for al-Ma'mun). Proof is admired at court and needed for astronomy; most surveyors and architects still work by rule of thumb. Local: al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf ibn Matar; al-Abbas ibn Said al-Jawhari (commentary on Euclid, tries to prove the parallel postulate); the Banu Musa (young).
- **Pi and the measurement of the circle** [`pi_circle_measurement`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/pi_circle_measurement.md) — K3, use correct, make easy, accept high. Archimedes' 3 1/7 is standard; al-Khwarizmi's mensuration chapter also reports Indian rules for the circle. Better digits are of no practical use yet; the Banu Musa will later write on measuring plane and spherical figures. Local: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi. Elsewhere: India (Aryabhata, 3.1416); China (Zu Chongzhi).
- **Trigonometry** [`trigonometry`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/trigonometry.md) — K3, use correct, make easy, accept high. The Indian sine (jayb, from Sanskrit jya) has replaced Ptolemy's chords in the new tables. Habash al-Hasib is introducing tables of the 'shadow', our tangent and cotangent, in these years. Spherical trigonometry is still Ptolemy's and Menelaus' theorem. Local: Habash al-Hasib al-Marwazi; Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (sine tables in his zij).
- **Coordinate geometry and graphs of functions** [`coordinate_geometry`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/coordinate_geometry.md) — K1, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Places are fixed by longitude and latitude, in Ptolemy's Geography and in al-Khwarizmi's coordinate list for a map of the world. Graphing a relation between two quantities is unknown. Local: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (Kitab surat al-ard).
- **Non-Euclidean geometry** [`non_euclidean_geometry`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/non_euclidean_geometry.md) — K0, use none, make easy, accept low. Doubt about the parallel postulate is just beginning; al-Jawhari attempts a proof of it in this period. Local: al-Abbas ibn Said al-Jawhari.
- **Linear perspective and technical drawing** [`perspective_technical_drawing`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/perspective_technical_drawing.md) — K1, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Builders draw plans on plaster or paper and work from cubit grids; painting is flat and figurative work is shunned in mosques. Euclid's Optics on visual rays is translated, but no one draws from it.
- **Surveying, levelling and triangulation** [`surveying_triangulation`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/surveying_triangulation.md) — K3, use correct, make easy, accept high. Canal engineers (muhandisun) level with water levels and sighting staffs for the Sawad's irrigation grid, a craft inherited from the Sasanians. Al-Ma'mun's astronomers measure a degree of meridian in the desert by rope and star altitude, about 56 2/3 Arabic miles. Local: muhandisun of the canal administration; Khalid ibn Abd al-Malik al-Marwarrudhi and Ali ibn Isa al-Asturlabi (degree measurement).
- **Solar calendar with leap years** [`solar_calendar_leap_years`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/solar_calendar_leap_years.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept low. The Hijri year is lunar and cannot be changed. Kharaj is collected by the Persian solar year of 365 days with no leap day, so Nawruz and the tax date drift through the seasons and farmers are taxed before harvest. Syriac Christians keep the Julian year with its leap day. Local: katibs of the diwan of the kharaj; Catholicos of the Church of the East (Julian computus).
- **Decimal, coherent system of units (metric system)** [`metric_system_units`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/metric_system_units.md) — K0, use none, make medium, accept low. Weights and measures are many and local; the dirham and mithqal set weights for coin, and the muhtasib in the market checks scales. The caliph could impose a standard, but every province would ignore it. Local: muhtasib (market inspector); mint at Madinat al-Salam.
- **Probability and statistics** [`probability_statistics`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/probability_statistics.md) — K0, use none, make easy, accept low. Games of chance are forbidden (maysir); nard and chess are played anyway. Al-Kindi will later break ciphers by counting letter frequencies; in 830 nobody reasons about chance. Local: Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi.
- **Bayes' theorem (updating belief by evidence)** [`bayes_theorem`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/bayes_theorem.md) — K0, use none, make easy, accept low
- **Errors of measurement, the bell curve and least squares** [`normal_distribution_errors`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/normal_distribution_errors.md) — K1, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Al-Ma'mun's astronomers repeat solstice and equinox observations because single ones disagree, and compare instruments. Choosing between values is by judgement; there is no theory of error. Local: Yahya ibn Abi Mansur and Sanad ibn Ali (Shammasiyya).
- **Graphs of data (line, bar and pie charts)** [`data_graphs`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/data_graphs.md) — K0, use none, make easy, accept medium. Tables (zij) are the form of data. Paper is plentiful, so a chart of Tigris levels or prices could be drawn by any copyist.
- **Calculus (differentiation and integration)** [`calculus`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/calculus.md) — K0, use none, make hard, accept low. Archimedes' exhaustion methods reach Arabic only partly and later; Euclid book 12 is the furthest anyone goes.
